questions.question: A girl has a battery, a bulb and a single wire. She holds one end of the wire to the top of the battery and the other end to the metal base of the bulb, and nothing else touches. Why does the bulb stay dark?
questions.answer: The electricity has no path back to the battery
choices: The electricity has no path back to the battery
One wire is too thin to carry enough electricity
The electricity needs a switch to start it flowing
The electricity is used up inside the wire
questions.context: Electricity flows only round a complete loop: out of one end of the battery, through the bulb, and back into the other end. With nothing leading back, no electricity flows at all, so none is used up, and a switch is not needed to start it. If the tip of the bulb's base also touches the battery's other end, even one wire can light it.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.8B has 5th graders identify what a working circuit needs, a complete loop, and NSTA's one-wire probe finds the single-wire idea that this corrects.

questions.question: A boy switches on his flashlight, and the bulb lights up. What has happened inside the switch?
questions.answer: Metal touched metal and closed the circuit
choices: Metal touched metal and closed the circuit
Metal touched metal and opened the circuit
Plastic touched plastic and closed the circuit
Plastic touched plastic and opened the circuit
questions.context: A switch brings two metal parts together or pulls them apart. Turned on, they touch and close the circuit, so electricity can cross; turned off, they part and open it, leaving a gap. The words run opposite to a door's: an open door lets people through, but an open switch lets no electricity through, and plastic could never carry it across.
questions.grade_note: Oak National Academy's Year 6 (ages 10 to 11) circuits unit teaches that a switch works by making two conductors touch or separate, and TEKS 5.8B has 5th graders identify what a working circuit needs.

questions.question: A boy joins a battery, a bulb and a switch in one loop of wire. The switch sits on the far side of the bulb, on the wire leading back to the battery. With the bulb glowing, he turns the switch off. What happens to the bulb?
questions.answer: It goes out, for the loop is broken
choices: It goes out, for the loop is broken
It stays lit, for the gap lies beyond it
It dims, for the switch lets less through
It glows on until the wire runs empty
questions.context: Turning the switch off opens a gap, and a gap anywhere in a single loop stops the electricity all the way round at once. The switch works the same before the bulb or after it, and no electricity waits in the wire to keep the bulb glowing.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.8B's requirements for a working circuit include that an open switch or any break stops the current, and primary guides list 'a switch after the bulb cannot turn it off' as a common mistake.

questions.question: The wires inside a house's walls and in a lamp's cord carry electricity along a core of one metal. It is chosen because it conducts electricity very well and bends easily without cracking. Which metal is it?
choices: Copper
Iron
Silver
Gold
questions.context: Copper conducts electricity better than every metal except silver, and silver costs fifty to a hundred times as much. Gold conducts less well than copper, and iron only about a sixth as well. The tall power lines strung between towers are mostly aluminium, which is lighter.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade circuit units name copper and other metals as the conductors that wires are made of (map line G5.P6, TEKS 5.6A), and copper wire is the standard example.

questions.question: The metal wire in a lamp's cord is wrapped from end to end in a coat of plastic. What is the plastic coat for?
questions.answer: It keeps electricity from reaching a hand
choices: It keeps electricity from reaching a hand
It helps electricity flow along the wire faster
It slows electricity down to a safe speed
It stores some electricity for the lamp
questions.context: Plastic is an insulator: it does not let electricity pass, so it keeps the current inside the metal wire and away from anyone who touches the cord. It does not change how the current flows in the wire, and it stores none. A cord whose plastic has cracked, with bare wire showing, is dangerous to touch.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.6A and map line G5.P6 have 5th graders compare conductors and insulators of electricity, and that wires are coated in plastic to keep people safe is the grade's standard example.

questions.question: Power lines strung between tall steel towers carry a great deal of electricity, yet none of it runs down the towers into the ground. What stops it?
questions.answer: Insulators hold the lines away from the steel
choices: Insulators hold the lines away from the steel
Steel does not let electricity pass through it
The electricity moves too fast to turn aside
Rubber pads under the towers block it
questions.context: The lines are bare metal, and each hangs from insulators of glass, porcelain or tough plastic, which hold it away from the tower so that no electricity can cross into the steel. Steel is a metal and conducts electricity well, which is why the lines must be kept from touching it.
questions.grade_note: Map line G5.P6 has 5th graders learn what insulators such as glass do in a circuit, and the insulators on power towers are an everyday use of them.

questions.question: A woman runs a bath from the tap. Tap water carries tiny amounts of minerals dissolved in it. What does this water do with electricity?
questions.answer: It lets electricity pass through it
choices: It lets electricity pass through it
It blocks electricity, as rubber does
It soaks up electricity and holds it
It pulls electricity in, like a magnet
questions.context: The dissolved minerals let tap water carry electricity, though perfectly pure water barely lets any through. So nothing with a plug is used beside a bath, a sink or a pool, and wet hands are dried before they touch a switch.
questions.grade_note: Electrical-safety lessons at this grade teach that water and electricity must be kept apart, and Oak's primary lessons (ages 8 to 11) teach that minerals dissolved in water conduct electricity.

questions.question: A crow flies up to a power line high on a steel tower and perches with both feet on that one line. It is not hurt. Why not?
questions.answer: It is not part of a complete loop
choices: It is not part of a complete loop
The line is wrapped in a coat of plastic
A bird's body does not let electricity through
The line's electricity is too weak to hurt it
questions.context: Electricity flows only round a complete loop, and a bird touching just one line gives it no path through its body. A bird that touches two lines at once, or a line and a tower, does complete a loop and can be killed, for the lines are bare metal and carry deadly electricity.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.8B has 5th graders identify that a circuit must be a complete loop, and the bird on a power line applies it to the power-line safety the grade is taught.

questions.question: Electricity flows only along an unbroken path: out of one end of a battery, along wires and through a bulb, then back into the battery's other end. What is this whole path called?
choices: A circuit
A current
A conductor
A cable
questions.context: The circuit is the whole path; the current is the electricity flowing along it; a conductor is a material, such as copper, that lets electricity flow. A cable is only a bundle of wires in one coat, just one part of a circuit.
questions.grade_note: The circuit as a closed path that electricity travels round is the core term of TEKS 5.8B, the 5th-grade standard on complete circuits.
